rv.q: Soldiers of Tomorrow emerges as an illuminating, embracing hour of political theatre nonetheless.

I feel like I have fairly normie bleeding heart European liberal views on Israel and its treatment of Palestine and as such I found leftwing Israeli performer Itai Erdal’s storytelling piece about his time in the IDF relatively uncontroversial.

The format of a monologue gives power to the narrator, whilst denying the same to every other character involved. The narration jumps between loose threads, bombarding the audience with snippets of history and flashbacks from a past life, the most powerful being his description of Gaza as the largest open prison in the world.

Sent to man infantry checkpoints in Lebanon, he sets out to do exactly what his mother tells him: “be kind to people”. That is no easy task when people are shooting at you, and Erdal struggles in vain to hold on to his faith that the IDF is “the most moral military in the world”.
In the end, Soldiers of Tomorrow may prove a little too reflective to convincingly grapple with the big questions it raises, let alone suggest any answers.
Engaging in a moral debate that goes beyond the Israeli-Arab dichotomy, this is a sobering meditation.
It’s performed with a bright, ringing confidence by de Nordwall that suggests it certainly means something to her but it fails to communicate much more than a lingering sense of befuddlement.

cn.t: Erdal's thoughtful storytelling piece about his experiences in the Israeli Defence Force earns praise for discussing a difficult topic with warmth, wit, and nuance, enhanced by live music and striking visual design.
